thread.title: Markets Drop on Renewed Trade Threats. Is This Now War?

author: François Auré
title: Markets Drop on Renewed Trade Threats. Is This Now War?
text:
Markets Drop On Renewed Trade Threats. Is This Now War? Markets Drop On Renewed Trade Threats. Is This Now War? Facebook Trade tensions are at levels where we can probably call the situation a trade war. Markets have been resilient through most of 2018, but this week saw some of the outperforming Tech stocks finally break down. Things have the potential to get a whole lot worse as US initiatives to restrict Tech investments could spark a retaliation from China.
Trade tensions have been around for the majority of 2018, but most commentators were keen to point out the situation was not bad enough to label it a “trade war”. However, in light of recent developments, this has begun to change. Already last week Danske Bank told us “we have now entered what we would call a trade war as the tit-for-tat reactions are escalating.” And that was before markets were rocked by tweets from President Trump aimed at “all countries” which threatened “reciprocity” from the US unless they remove trade barriers and tariffs. The US also piled more pressure on China as it threatened to restrict investment in US Tech firms.
“In the latest escalation of the trade war Trump has decided to take aim at Chinese investments. A draft series of restrictions on inbound Chinese investments are due to be published later this week, in a move which could have great long-term consequences on the US – Sino economic relationship,” commented Politico.
Such actions are aimed specifically at hurting Chinese developments in technology. US companies have the clear lead in Tech, but are being caught up by Chinese firms. Here’s the WSJ with more,
“The twin initiatives, set to be announced by the end of the week, are designed to prevent Beijing from moving ahead with plans outlined in its “made in China 2025” report to become a global leader in 10 broad areas of technology.
The Treasury Department is crafting rules that would block firms with at least 25% Chinese ownership from buying companies involved in what the White House calls “industrially significant technology.”
The ceiling may end up lower than that, according to people familiar with discussions finalizing the plans.”
This will not only restrict Chinese practices, but will end much needed investment. In 2016, Chinese companies made a record $46bn in direct investment in the US, much in smaller start-ups. Cutting off this source of funding could hurt the US too.
And that’s just the start. If the initiatives described by the WSJ were imposed, China would almost certainly retaliate and that could mean clampdowns on U.S. technology firms active in China. Watch out Apple (AAPL). Going the Whole Hog
As a backdrop to the Tech race and tit for tat actions, an older, more traditional industry is also under pressure. Harley Davidson was specifically targeted for increased tariffs by the EU as it would hurt Trump in key states. They have now announced they will have to move more production to europp to remain competitive.
“Increasing international production to alleviate the EU tariff burden is not the company’s preference, but represents the only sustainable option to make its motorcycles accessible to customers in the EU and maintain a viable business in Europe,” a company spokesperson said.
President Trump was unhappy about this decision, but with Harley Davidson motorcycles costing $2.2k more in Europe due to the tariffs, it seems the company has little choice. Market Reaction
As may be expected, markets have been risk averse to start the week, with massive moves down in Tech names and the Nasdaq. Netflix – usually an outperforming stock – was down 7% at one point on Monday. Yen was well bid, but unusually gold stayed weak throughout. Dollar pairs were broadly unmoved, with EURUSD holding onto the reversal made late last week despite lackluster IFO data.
Tuesday has seen a slight recovery so far, but it seems the market is waiting for the US open and whether the sell off will resume. Advertisement
